title: A vaccine made from your own tumour cuts melanoma's return
dek: After more than a century of failures, a personalised mRNA cancer vaccine has succeeded in a large trial. Big questions remain.

article: A personalised vaccine built from a patient's own tumour has cut the risk of skin cancer returning, in what experts call the first late-stage success for a cancer-treating vaccine after more than a century of failed attempts.

The treatment, called intismeran and developed by Moderna and Merck, uses mRNA - the same technology behind Moderna's Covid-19 vaccine. mRNA works like a set of instructions that tells cells which proteins to make. Here, the instructions describe proteins found only on the patient's cancer cells, so that the immune system learns to recognise them and attack.

The process starts after surgery. Doctors sequence the removed tumour to find its unique mutations, and Moderna then manufactures a vaccine aimed at 34 of them. Because it is custom-made, it can target dozens of mutations at once, whereas earlier vaccines that aimed at just one or two failed.

The trial involved 1,137 people whose melanoma, the deadliest form of skin cancer, had been surgically removed. All received Keytruda, a standard drug that helps immune cells fight cancer; 757 also received the vaccine, while 380 received a placebo. Adding the vaccine reduced the risk of the cancer returning or of death by 42%, and the risk of it spreading by 38%, compared with Keytruda alone. Reported side effects included soreness where the injection was given.

Melanoma was a deliberate choice. Its tumours carry an unusually high number of mutations, giving the vaccine plenty of targets, and treating patients at an early stage left time to make each custom vaccine.

That choice also marks the limits of the result. The approach is untested in cancers with fewer mutations, such as lung, kidney and pancreatic cancer. Full results have not yet appeared in a peer-reviewed journal, and researchers do not yet know whether the vaccine helps patients live longer.

Even so, the findings have raised hopes well beyond medicine. Moderna's shares more than doubled after the results, and regulators in the US are reviewing the treatment, with approval possible as soon as next year. The two companies are already testing it in other cancers.
For a field long defined by disappointment, a vaccine that teaches the body to recognise its own disease may finally be moving from promise to practice.

tasks.q: Which headline best sums up the WHOLE article?
options: Personalised mRNA vaccine cuts melanoma's return in large trial, but key questions remain
Scientists find a cure for every kind of cancer
Covid-19 vaccines can now prevent skin cancer
tasks.explain: B is an overclaim (paragraph 6: untested in other cancers). C is a single detail from paragraph 7. D distorts paragraph 2: the vaccine only shares the mRNA technology with the Covid-19 vaccine.

tasks.q: Put the treatment steps in order (paragraphs 2-4).
items: Doctors sequence it to find its unique mutations
Moderna makes a vaccine aimed at 34 of them
The patient receives the vaccine together with Keytruda
The immune system learns to recognise the cancer cells
tasks.explain: "The process starts after surgery" (paragraph 3) gives you the first step; the purpose - teaching the immune system - is explained in paragraph 2.

tasks.q: Scan the article: what does each number refer to?

pairs.right: lower risk of the cancer returning or death
lower risk of the cancer spreading

tasks.explain: 757 + 380 = 1,137 - a quick check that you matched the trial numbers correctly.

statements.text: Every patient in the trial received Keytruda.
The vaccine has been shown to help patients live longer.
statements.explain: Paragraph 6: researchers "do not yet know" whether it helps patients live longer.

statements.text: The vaccine costs less than Keytruda.
The approach has already worked in pancreatic cancer.
statements.explain: Paragraph 6: it is untested in cancers such as pancreatic cancer.

statements.text: Most patients in the trial were over 60.
statements.explain: Patients' ages are not given anywhere.

tasks.q: Why might the vaccine work less well in cancers with fewer mutations?
options: There would be fewer unique targets for the immune system to learn
Those cancers cannot be removed by surgery
Keytruda does not exist for those cancers
tasks.explain: Paragraph 5 says melanoma's many mutations give "plenty of targets". Fewer mutations means fewer targets. B, C and D are never said.

tasks.q: In paragraph 5, "Melanoma was a deliberate choice" means it was:
options: chosen on purpose, for good reasons
chosen because it is the most common cancer
tasks.explain: The next sentence gives the reasons for the choice (many mutations, time to make the vaccine), so it was planned - deliberate.

tasks.q: What is the main job of paragraph 6?
options: To point out the limits of the result
To describe the side effects of the vaccine
To show that the trial was a failure
tasks.explain: Its first sentence says it: "That choice also marks the limits of the result." D goes too far - the trial succeeded, it just did not answer every question.

write.prompt: If you were a doctor, would you recommend this vaccine to a patient now, or wait for more results? Write 2-3 sentences in English and give one reason.
write.sample: I would recommend it to high-risk melanoma patients once it is approved, because it lowered the risk of the cancer returning. However, I would explain that it is still untested in other cancers and that we do not yet know if it helps people live longer.
